clue.text: Dream that involved someone in Wonderland

indicators.note: involved means tangled or intricate, telling us to tangle these two words into a new order

explanation.surface: A dream that featured a character from Lewis Carroll's Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's riddling host of the mad tea party, with his oversized hat, is a character Alice meets in Wonderland.

clue.text: Time lock, we hear, at 4

parts.note: March is a month, a period of time

indicators.note: we hear signals that a word is to be taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: a lock is a strand from the head

explanation.surface: A timed lock that, people say, opens at four o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: The 4 is a cross-reference to 4-down, TEA PARTY: 'at 4' means one of the guests at that party in Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's long-eared creature sits with the Hatter and the Dormouse as a guest at the mad tea party.

clue.text: Takes in money in subscriptions

indicators.note: in tells us one piece is placed inside the other here

parts.note: dues are regular subscriptions paid to a club or society
P, for penny, is a common abbreviation standing for money

explanation.surface: A society collects cash from its membership fees.
explanation.definitionFit: To trick or fool someone is to take them in, a phrasal verb.

clue.text: Before imbibing I ordered a drink

indicators.note: imbibing means drinking in, so one piece swallows the other pieces

parts.note: ante is Latin for before, familiar from ante-room and antenatal
set can mean arranged or put in order

explanation.surface: Before drinking anything, I ordered a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: An aniseed-flavoured liqueur is a kind of drink.

clue.text: Social event in Boston

parts.note: read plainly, a gathering in a Boston drawing room; it also recalls the 1773 protest in which colonists dumped chests of leaves into Boston harbour

explanation.definitionFit: An afternoon gathering over cups and cakes is a social event, and the 1773 protest against British taxes in Boston harbour bears the same name.

clue.text: Discount notes in value

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other piece

parts.note: rate as in the going rate, a value or price
E and B are musical notes

explanation.surface: Banknotes offered at a discount on their face value.
explanation.definitionFit: A partial refund on a payment amounts to a discount.

clue.text: Wet — one in the majority

indicators.note: in puts the numeral inside the other piece

parts.note: most means the greater part, the majority
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Rainy weather, and one voter is in the majority.
explanation.definitionFit: Something damp is slightly wet.

clue.text: Married woman showing spile

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for married, as in family trees
Alice is a woman's name, fitting the Wonderland theme

explanation.surface: A wife displaying spite.
explanation.walkthrough: Alice is also the heroine of the puzzle's Wonderland theme, so the name is a natural pick for 'woman'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spite and ill will are the same desire to hurt someone.

clue.text: Ask about leaders of organisations — lots are unsullied

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other letters

parts.note: to ask someone along is to invite them

indicators.note: leaders are the front letters, here of three consecutive words

explanation.surface: Questioning the heads of organisations, many turn out to be clean.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'lots are unsullied' read as a separate statement, but 'lots' and 'are' still give their front letters along with organisations.
explanation.definitionFit: Something kept pure and unbroken, never violated, is unsullied.

clue.text: Without the others, they risked being short

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as printed and scanned, 'Without the others, they risked being short (5)', gives no wordplay for TERSE that uses every word; no source found for a sounder version
annotationWithheld.clue: Without the others, they risked being short

clue.text: Salesman left in charge takes a copy

parts.note: rep is short for sales representative
IC is short for in charge, as in 2IC, second in command

explanation.surface: A salesman left minding the shop picks up a facsimile.
explanation.definitionFit: An exact reproduction of something is a copy.

clue.text: Liberator worth 100 centimos

explanation.surface: A freedom fighter valued at a hundred cents.
explanation.definitionFit: Venezuela's independence hero Simón was called the Liberator, and the country's currency unit, named after him, divides into 100 céntimos.

clue.text: Expedition starts to hurry as summer time ends

indicators.note: starts to signals the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A trip begins to rush as the summer holidays draw to a close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' looks like a journey but here is its older sense of speed, as in 'with all expedition'.
explanation.definitionFit: Expedition in its older sense means promptness or speed of action.

clue.text: Take choir abroad — Jerusalem, perhaps?

indicators.note: abroad can mean astray or scattered, so these letters wander into a new order

explanation.surface: Taking a church choir on tour overseas, maybe to the Holy Land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerusalem' is not the city: it names a variety of a vegetable, a definition by example, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jerusalem variety is a knobbly edible tuber, one type of this vegetable.

clue.text: A renegade, an airman, say

parts.note: PO is a Pilot Officer, a rank in Britain's Royal Air Force, so an airman
to state something is to say it

explanation.surface: Calling a pilot a turncoat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' looks like the usual 'for example' signal; here it is a verb meaning declare. PO, Pilot Officer, is a junior RAF officer rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who abandons their faith or cause is a renegade.

clue.text: In addition, he's done it wrong

indicators.note: wrong suggests the letters have been put together badly and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Blaming someone for a botched job: he's done it wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means as an extra, beyond the main job or order, so in addition.

clue.text: Perhaps a club's race programme

explanation.surface: A sports club's programme for its race day.
explanation.walkthrough: A club is one of the four suits in a pack; a race programme is the printed list of runners and times at a British race meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: A club is an example of a playing piece from a pack, and the printed list of runners at a race meeting has the same name.

clue.text: Refuse to believe the record having, so to speak, studied it

parts.note: a disc is a gramophone record

indicators.note: so to speak signals that the words are to be heard rather than read

parts.note: to have read it means to have studied it

explanation.surface: Doubting the record after having looked into it.
explanation.walkthrough: READ IT is past tense, said 'red it', and the second half of the answer is spelt as it sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: To reject a claim as untrue is to refuse to believe it.

clue.text: Breaking into pieces. I attracted an adherent

indicators.note: breaking into means forcing a way inside, so one piece enters the other

parts.note: parts are pieces

explanation.surface: Something smashes to pieces, and I won over a follower.
explanation.definitionFit: A committed supporter of a party or cause is an adherent.

clue.text: 4's guest room used differently

indicators.note: differently means arranged in another way, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: The tea party visitor gets a room that has been put to another use.
explanation.walkthrough: 4 is a cross-reference to 4-down, the mad tea party in Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's sleepy little rodent, dozing between the Hatter and the long-eared host, is a guest at the mad tea party.

clue.text: Cockney warms up food

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: to heat something is to warm it up

explanation.surface: A Londoner reheats dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney, the dialect of working-class East London, drops initial H, so the word loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal slang for grub or meals, as on a sign outside a roadside café.

clue.text: Woman holding another back — that's noble!

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the first name grips the second

parts.note: Bess is a woman's name, short for Elizabeth

indicators.note: back says this second name is written in reverse

parts.note: Nora is another woman's name

explanation.surface: A woman restraining another, praised for her noble act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'noble' looks like an adjective praising the act; it is the noun, a member of the peerage, which the woman in the answer is.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman with a title in the peerage, ranking above a viscountess's lower neighbours, is a noble.

clue.text: Give instruction in class

parts.note: a form is a school class in Britain

explanation.surface: A teacher giving a lesson in the classroom.
explanation.definitionFit: To tell someone facts or pass on knowledge is to give instruction.

clue.text: Things thrown out from planes over America

indicators.note: over in a down clue means the first piece sits above the next

parts.note: jets are jet aircraft, planes

explanation.surface: Items dropped from aircraft flying over the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Cargo dumped overboard from a ship to lighten it is things thrown out.

clue.text: Open country where golf balls may be seen hit hard

parts.words: where golf balls may be seen
parts.note: a green is the putting surface where golf balls end up
to belt something is to hit it hard

explanation.surface: A golf course where the balls get struck hard.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain this is the protected rural land around a town where building is restricted.
explanation.definitionFit: The protected ring of fields and woods kept free of building round a British city is open country.

clue.text: Total number

explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means total before deductions, as with income, and as a noun it is the number 144, a dozen dozen.

clue.text: Penny-pincher takes only half a seat in the stalls

indicators.note: only half means just the front half of the word is used

parts.note: a misericord is the hinged ledge seat in church choir stalls

explanation.surface: A skinflint pays for just half a seat in the theatre stalls.
explanation.walkthrough: The stalls are church choir stalls, not theatre seats; the misericord is the tip-up ledge there, and its first five letters are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: A stingy hoarder of money is a penny-pincher.

clue.text: Only about five find the answer

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the numeral

parts.note: sole means only, as in the sole survivor
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Only about five people can work out the puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: To work out a puzzle or problem is to find the answer.

clue.text: Domino used in part foreshadowing disaster

indicators.note: in part says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A domino played in a game portends catastrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: Something threatening or portentous foreshadows disaster.

clue.text: Neglected to include Light Infantry in the formation

indicators.note: to include means to take in, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: a squad is a small military formation
LI is the abbreviation for Light Infantry

explanation.surface: Someone failed to put the Light Infantry into the battle formation.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirty and run-down through lack of care means neglected.

clue.text: Cook takes the way back West …

parts.note: ST is short for street, a way

indicators.note: back means the name is written backwards

parts.note: Mae West was the American film actress, so West can stand for her first name

explanation.surface: A chef heads back along the road to the west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West' looks like a compass point but stands for Mae West, the 1930s Hollywood star; the ellipsis only links the surface to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To cook food in the vapour over boiling water is one way to cook.

clue.text: … meantime chefs beginning, cooking something to eat

indicators.note: cooking suggests the letters are stirred up and transformed
beginning picks out the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Meanwhile, the chefs are starting to cook something for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning' gives C from chefs, and 'cooking' mixes it with MEANTIME.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet spiced fruit filling of Christmas pies is something to eat.
